newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan Inc set for better earnings next fiscal year.
newsitem.headline: Japan Inc set for better earnings next fiscal year.

text.p: Japan Inc is seen enjoying healthy profit growth of above 10 percent next business year, as robust exports helped by the weak yen should absorb any damage from a planned sales tax hike, analysts said on Friday.

"Even though temporary repercussions from a planned sales tax hike and the end of an extraordinary income tax break are inevitable, the yen's decline will be significantly positive," Yamaichi Research Institute said in a report.

A set of reports by private research institutes released this week showed that current profits at Japan's leading firms are expected to grow by around 11 percent in 1997/98 after an estimated rise of just below 10 percent the previous year. Current profit is pre-tax and includes losses and gains on investments.
Profit forecasts generally do not include financial institutions, which are still expected to continue to struggle with their huge problem loans.
Yamaichi said that the automobile industry will continue to lead Japanese industry through early 1998.
Japan is set to raise the national sales tax rate to five percent from the current three percent on April 1 and end special income tax cuts totalling two trillion yen ($16.5 billion) this year.
The tax hike could temporarily put a damper on already feeble consumer confidence and thus hit sales of retailers.
Many firms will be unable to cushion consumers -- as some did when the tax was introduced eight years ago -- and will be forced to pass on the bigger tax burden by raising prices.
But the possible negative impact will be offset by the weak yen, which should bolster profits of export-oriented car and electronics makers by boosting their export incomes.
Many institutes used a dollar/yen rate of around 120 yen in calculating the profit forecasts. The dollar on Friday stood at 121 yen, compared with its year-ago level of around 106 yen.
Corporate profits have been aided by the yen's weakness, which makes Japanese products more price-competitive abroad, and by record low interest rates at home, analysts said.

"The weak yen and a likely end to inventory drawdowns (in the semiconductor, steel and oil industries) will become a major factor behind the expected profit rally next fiscal year," Daiwa Research Institute said in a report.
Daiwa saw parent current profits at Japan's leading firms growing an average of 12.0 percent, after estimated profit growth of 9.7 percent in the previous year.

Cash-strapped steel makers, which have long suffered from sluggish steel market prices, will finally see some improvement in their businesses as their restructuring efforts finally bear fruit this year, the institutes said.
Steelmakers are considered a bellwether for Japan's industrial health and their better earnings results could be taken as a sign of a stronger economic recovery.
On Thursday, Japan's five top steelmakers said their current profits may rise slightly in 1997/98 because of cost cutting and the weaker yen, which helped export sales.
Four out of the five companies also predicted that their profits for this fiscal year would be higher than their actual year-ago profits.
The recovering global semiconductor market, meanwhile, may work in favour of chipmakers, Nikko Research Centre said.

Spot prices for 16 megabit dynamic random access memory (DRAM) chips -- the current mainstay products used in PCs -- have gone up to around $9 from its level of around $6 earlier this year, industry sources said.

"Japan's top five electronics giants revised up their profit forecasts sharply, with their semiconductor divisions seen turning profits on the stabilising market and higher volume (in demand)," the Nikko report said. ($1=121 yen)
